entities.name: Galileo Galilei
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was an Italian astronomer, physicist, and mathematician — the 'father of modern science' (Einstein). In 1609, he built a telescope and turned it skyward, discovering Jupiter's four largest moons, Venus's phases, sunspots, lunar craters, and the Milky Way's individual stars.

These observations, published in Sidereus Nuncius (1610), provided the first empirical evidence for Copernicus's heliocentric model and demolished 1,400 years of Aristotelian-Ptolemaic cosmology.

His Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632) was so persuasive that the Inquisition convicted him of heresy (1633), forcing recantation and house arrest. Legend holds he muttered 'Eppur si muove' ('And yet it moves').

During house arrest, though blind, he produced his greatest work: Two New Sciences (1638), laying the foundations of kinematics and materials science. Stephen Hawking was born exactly 300 years after Galileo's death.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Galileo's observations provided empirical evidence for Copernicus's heliocentric model, challenging 1,400 years of Aristotelian-Ptolemaic cosmology and paving the way for modern astronomy. His work had far-reaching consequences for scientific inquiry and the development of Western philosophy.
